text:
Predicates:
Employee(x) ::: x is an employee.
SchedulesMeeting(x, y) ::: x schedules a meeting with y.
InCompanyBuilding(x) ::: x is in the company building.
HasLunch(x, y) ::: x has lunch at location y.
RemotelyFromHome(x) ::: x works remotely from home.
Manager(x) ::: x is a manager.
InOtherCountry(x) ::: x works in another country.
James ::: James.

Premises:
∀x (Employee(x) ∧ SchedulesMeeting(x, y) → InCompanyBuilding(x)) ::: All employees who schedule a meeting with their customers will go to the company building today.
∀x (HasLunch(x, company) → SchedulesMeeting(x, y)) ::: Everyone who has lunch in the company building schedules meetings with their customers.
∀x (HasLunch(x, home) ∨ InCompanyBuilding(x)) ::: Employees have lunch either in the company building or at home.
∀x (HasLunch(x, home) → RemotelyFromHome(x)) ::: If an employee has lunch at home, they are working remotely from home.
∀x (InOtherCountry(x) → RemotelyFromHome(x)) ::: All employees who are in other countries work remotely from home.
¬Manager(x) ::: No managers work remotely from home.
James ::: James.

Conclusion:
((Manager(James) ∨ InOtherCountry(James)) → ¬(HasLunch(James, home) ∨ RemotelyFromHome(James))) ::: If James is either a manager or in other countries, then James does not either have lunch at home or work remotely from home.
((HasLunch(James, home) ∨ RemotelyFromHome(James)) → ¬Manager(James) ∧ ¬InOtherCountry(James)) ::: If James either has lunch at home or works remotely from home, then he is neither a manager nor does he work in other countries.
